fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roles/2: First great systematic theologian of the church
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/summary: A Greek from Smyrna who had heard Polycarp, Irenaeus became bishop of Lyon after the persecution of 177. His Against Heresies refuted the Valentinian Gnostics and Marcion by appealing to the one God who is both Creator and Redeemer, the 'rule of truth', the public succession of bishops and a fourfold Gospel. His theology of 'recapitulation', in which Christ sums up and heals the human story, deeply shaped Eastern and Western theology.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/story:
Irenaeus was born in Smyrna c. 130–140, where as a boy he heard Polycarp tell of John and others who had seen the Lord. He migrated to southern Gaul, probably with other Christians from Asia Minor, and became a presbyter in Lugdunum (Lyon), the Roman capital of the Three Gauls. In 177 the churches of Lyon and Vienne sent him to Rome with a letter to Bishop Eleutherus about the Montanist 'New Prophecy'. During his absence a violent persecution killed the aged bishop Pothinus, Blandina and many others; Irenaeus returned to succeed Pothinus.

His main work, 'The Refutation and Overthrow of Knowledge Falsely So Called', known as Against Heresies (c. 180–189), survives complete only in an early Latin translation, with Greek fragments and an Armenian version of books 4–5. Book 1 describes Valentinian and other Gnostic systems in detail, an account the Nag Hammadi discoveries (1945) have shown to be broadly accurate though polemical. Books 2–5 refute them from reason, the apostolic tradition, the sayings of the Lord and the Pauline letters. His shorter Demonstration of the Apostolic Preaching, rediscovered in Armenian in 1904, is a catechetical summary of the faith.

Against teachers who claimed a secret tradition, Irenaeus pointed to the public faith of the churches: a 'rule of truth' received at baptism, taught everywhere the same, and guarded by bishops in succession from the apostles, illustrated by the list of Roman bishops from Linus to Eleutherus. He wrote that every church must agree with Rome 'on account of its more powerful origin' (propter potentiorem principalitatem, 3.3.2), a phrase whose meaning is still debated. He argued that there can be only four Gospels, as there are four winds and four living creatures (3.11.8), the first clear defence of a fixed fourfold Gospel.

Irenaeus's positive theology is a grand narrative of salvation. The one God creates through his 'two hands', the Son and the Spirit; humanity is made in God's image as a child meant to grow into his likeness; Adam falls, but Christ 'recapitulates' (anakephalaiosis, Ephesians 1:10) the whole human story, undoing disobedience by obedience, as Mary's obedience unties the knot of Eve's. 'The glory of God is a living human being, and the life of humanity is the vision of God' (4.20.7); the Son 'became what we are, that he might bring us to be what he is' (5, preface). The Eucharist, as the bread of the earth made Christ's body, is proof of the resurrection of the flesh. He was also a millenarian (5.32–36).

Around 190 he wrote to Pope Victor, who had excommunicated the Asian churches over the date of Easter, urging peace and citing the precedent of Polycarp and Anicetus; Eusebius remarks that he lived up to his name (eirene, 'peace'). The date and manner of his death are unknown; a later tradition makes him a martyr c. 202. Venerated in East and West, he was declared a Doctor of the Church, with the title 'Doctor of Unity', by Pope Francis in January 2022.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roots/0/text: He grounds his theology in the teaching of the apostles handed down publicly, his own memory of Polycarp and the elders of Asia, and a broad canon of Gospels and Pauline letters.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roots/1/text: He draws on Justin Martyr (including a lost work against Marcion), Ignatius, 1 Clement, Polycarp and Papias, and on Theophilus of Antioch.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roots/2/text: His entire theology is shaped by refuting Valentinians, Basilidians, Marcion and others, defending the goodness of creation and the unity of God.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roots/3/text: Against Marcion he insists the God of the Law and prophets is the Father of Jesus, reading the whole Old Testament as a pedagogy leading to Christ.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/roots/4/text: He apologises for his lack of style, but uses the standard methods of rhetorical refutation and parody of his opponents' systems.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/0: One God, Creator and Father of Jesus Christ, against Gnostic and Marcionite dualism
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/1: The rule of truth (regula veritatis) and apostolic succession of bishops as guarantors of public teaching
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/3: Recapitulation: Christ sums up and restores humanity, the new Adam
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/4: Son and Spirit as the 'two hands' of God
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/5: Mary as the new Eve whose obedience undoes Eve's disobedience
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/keyTeachings/6: Growth from image to likeness; salvation as participation in God's life
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/works/0/note: Refutation of the Gnostics and exposition of apostolic faith; survives in Latin, with Greek and Armenian fragments.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/works/1/note: Short catechetical summary of salvation history; known only in an Armenian translation discovered in 1904.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/works/2/title: Letters to Florinus and to Victor of Rome
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/works/2/note: Fragments preserved by Eusebius on his memories of Polycarp and the Easter dispute.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/doctrineContrib: First clear defence of a fourfold Gospel and of Scripture read within the apostolic 'rule of truth'.
Developed the argument from public apostolic succession of bishops, especially at Rome.
Recapitulation and Christ's victory over sin and death; Aulén's Christus Victor treats him as the classic representative of this view.
Defended the goodness of the material creation and creation by the one God, without intermediaries.
His picture of Adam as an immature child growing towards maturity underlies the modern 'Irenaean theodicy' (John Hick).
Developed the Eve–Mary parallel, foundational for later Mariology.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/laterInfluence/: Tertullian, Hippolytus and Athanasius used his anti-heretical method and his theology of the incarnation and deification.
Read in the Latin West mainly through excerpts; his argument from Roman succession was cited in papal apologetics.
Erasmus published the first printed edition (1526); Reformers and Catholics both cited him in arguments over Scripture and tradition.
Highly valued for his doctrine of deification and his sense of salvation as the healing and growth of humanity.
Revived by ressourcement theologians (Daniélou, von Balthasar), the Lutheran Gustaf Wingren, Aulén's Christus Victor and Hick's Evil and the God of Love (1966).
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/reception/0/tex: Saint (feast 28 June); declared a Doctor of the Church ('Doctor of Unity') by Pope Francis on 21 January 2022.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/reception/1/tex: Hieromartyr Irenaeus, commemorated 23 August; honoured as a bridge between East and West.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/reception/2/tex: Commemorated on 28 June; his theology of recapitulation is widely used in modern Protestant theology.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/reception/3/tex: Respected as a defender of Scripture and orthodoxy against heresy; his appeal to episcopal succession is not accepted.
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/controversies/0: Meaning of the 'more powerful origin' (potentior principalitas) of the Roman church
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/controversies/1: Fairness and accuracy of his portrayal of the Gnostics
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/controversies/3: Whether he died as a martyr
fathers/irenaeus-of-lyon/quote/text: The glory of God is a living human being; and the life of humanity is the vision of God.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/summary: Titus Flavius Clemens, an Athenian-educated convert who taught in Alexandria c. 180–202, was the first Christian writer to set out a thorough programme for using Greek philosophy as a ‘preparation’ for the Gospel and to describe the mature Christian as the ‘true gnostic’.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/story:
Clement was probably born in Athens around 150 to a pagan family and received a full Greek education in literature and philosophy. After conversion he travelled in search of teachers through southern Italy, Syria and Palestine, finally finding ‘rest’ in Alexandria under a teacher usually identified with Pantaenus, a former Stoic whom Eusebius names as head of the Alexandrian catechetical school (Stromateis 1.1.11; Eusebius, Church History 5.11).

In Alexandria he taught educated converts and enquirers for some two decades. Whether there was yet a formal, church-sponsored ‘catechetical school’ in his day is debated; many historians now think Clement ran something closer to a private philosophical circle, and that Eusebius projects the later institution of Origen’s time back onto him. The persecution under Septimius Severus (c. 202–203) drove him from the city. He reappears in Cappadocia, where Bishop Alexander (later of Jerusalem) commends him in a letter of c. 211, and he was dead by about 215.

His surviving trilogy is a deliberate curriculum. The Protrepticus (Exhortation to the Greeks) mocks the mysteries and myths while quoting Homer, Plato and the poets to urge conversion to the Logos, the ‘new song’. The Paedagogus (Instructor) presents Christ as the tutor of the newly baptised, giving detailed and often Stoic-coloured advice on food, drink, dress and conduct. The Stromateis (‘Patchwork’ or ‘Miscellanies’) deliberately scatter deeper teaching among digressions, defending philosophy, faith and the ‘true gnosis’ against both anti-intellectual Christians and Valentinian Gnostics. Shorter works include Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?, the Excerpts from Theodotus and the Eclogae Propheticae.

Clement’s great theme is that the one divine Logos has been educating humanity throughout history: through the Law for the Jews and through philosophy for the Greeks, ‘a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind to Christ’ (Stromateis 1.5.28). He borrowed heavily from Philo of Alexandria (whom he calls ‘the Pythagorean’), from Middle Platonism and from Stoic ethics, while insisting that faith is the foundation of knowledge. His ideal of passionlessness (apatheia) and contemplative assimilation to God shaped later Eastern spirituality.

Clement was venerated as a saint in the West until the sixteenth century, when Pope Clement VIII’s revision of the Roman Martyrology (on the advice of Baronius) removed him because of doubts about his orthodoxy, citing Photius’ criticisms. He is honoured as a Father by Orthodox and Coptic Christians and widely read by Anglican and Protestant scholars as the classic early advocate of a positive relation between faith and reason.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/0/te: Clement is the first Christian to use Philo extensively, borrowing whole passages of allegorical exegesis (e.g. Hagar and Sarah as preparatory learning and wisdom) and Philo’s doctrine of the Logos as God’s mediating reason.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/1/te: His transcendent, unknowable God who is reached by abstraction and negation, and the ideal of ‘becoming like God’ (Plato, Theaetetus 176b), are taken from contemporary Middle Platonism.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/2/te: The Paedagogus draws on Stoic moralists such as Musonius Rufus for its practical ethics; apatheia and life ‘according to the Logos’ are Stoic ideals given a Christian meaning.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/3/te: The Stromateis argue against Valentinians and Basilideans that faith and knowledge are not two classes of Christians, reclaiming the word ‘gnostic’ for the mature orthodox believer.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/4/te: Clement argues, following Jewish apologists, that Moses was older than the Greek philosophers and that Plato ‘borrowed’ from him — the so-called theft theory.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/roots/5/te: A highly literary author, he quotes over 300 classical writers and writes in the cultivated style of the Second Sophistic.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/keyTeachin: Philosophy was given to the Greeks as a ‘schoolmaster’ to Christ, as the Law was to the Jews
Faith is the foundation of knowledge; the mature Christian is the ‘true gnostic’ who grows from faith to understanding and love
The Logos is creator, revealer and educator of the whole human race
Salvation as progressive education and assimilation to God, culminating in apatheia and contemplation
Wealth is not evil in itself; what matters is detachment and generous use (Who Is the Rich Man?)
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/0/no: Apologetic appeal ridiculing pagan myths and mysteries and inviting Greeks to the Logos.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/1/no: Christ as tutor; practical ethics for daily Christian life in a wealthy city.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/2/no: Eight books on faith, philosophy and the ‘true gnostic’; deliberately unsystematic.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/3/ti: Quis dives salvetur? (Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved?)
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/3/no: Homily on Mark 10 arguing that renunciation concerns the passions rather than possessions as such.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/works/4/no: Notes on a Valentinian teacher; an important source for Gnostic thought.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/doctrineCo: Developed the idea of philosophy as a providential preparation for the Gospel (praeparatio evangelica), later taken up by Eusebius.
Pioneered the ideals of contemplation, apatheia and deification that later shaped Eastern monastic spirituality.
Laid the foundations of the Alexandrian tradition of learned, allegorical and philosophically engaged theology.
Among the first to speak of deification: ‘the Logos of God became man so that you might learn from a man how a man may become God’ (Protrepticus 1.8).
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/laterInflu: Origen inherited Clement’s synthesis of scripture, allegory and Platonism and developed it into a systematic theology.
His language of apatheia and gnosis passes through Origen and Evagrius into Byzantine monastic theology.
Renaissance and Anglican humanists cited Clement as precedent for valuing classical learning.
Often invoked in discussions of inculturation and of ‘logos’ theologies of other religions.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/reception/: Removed from the Roman Martyrology in the 1580s–90s because of doubts about his orthodoxy; respected as a Father and early theologian but not venerated as a saint in the Roman calendar.
Read as an early Father; some local commemorations exist, though he is not universally listed among the saints.
Honoured as a teacher of the School of Alexandria and part of the Coptic church’s intellectual heritage.
Valued by scholars as an early model of engagement with culture, though criticised by some for over-Hellenising the faith.
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/controvers: Photius (9th century) accused his lost Hypotyposeis of errors on the Logos, matter and transmigration
Debate over whether his ‘true gnostic’ creates an elite tier of Christians
Adolf von Harnack’s thesis that Clement marks the ‘Hellenisation’ of Christianity
fathers/clement-of-alexandria/quote/text: Philosophy was a schoolmaster to bring the Hellenic mind, as the Law the Hebrews, to Christ.
